# Vertex-cluster mixtures and the projected-support parity obstruction

Let T be the standard 5-simplex, g its centroid, and Gamma_5=(5/6)^5.
An arbitrary integer-valued convex-body mixture can have exact ordinary
maximal depth 1/6<Gamma_5/2. The support of the example below cannot
be the projection of any one-integer-coordinate convex source. A general
parity argument then bounds such convex-position support clusters by
2^n in n integer dimensions.

## 1. Arbitrary mixtures can be below Gamma_5/2

Let v_0=0,v_i=e_i be the six vertices of T, and choose 0<delta<1/5.
Consider the six equal-volume disjoint convex clusters

    Q_i=v_i+delta(T-g),  i=0,...,5,
    sigma=sum_i 1_(Q_i).

Every x in Q_i has

    lambda_i(x)>=1-delta/6,
    lambda_j(x)<=5delta/6 for j!=i.                     (9)

Thus the canonical through-g caps {lambda_i>=1/6} each capture
exactly one whole cluster, and cover R^5. They prove D(sigma)<=1/6.

For the matching all-normal lower bound, let a nonzero through-g
linear margin take values h_i at the six vertices. Their sum is
zero. If m=max_i h_i>0, then every h_j>=-5m. In the cluster attached
to a maximizing vertex, every point has margin at least

    m+delta min_j h_j >=(1-5delta)m>0.

Hence every through-g halfspace contains a whole cluster. A containing
halfspace includes its parallel through-g halfspace. Therefore

    D(sigma)=1/6 < Gamma_5/2,
    Gamma_5/2-1/6=533/15552>0.                          (10)

The deepest point g need not belong to the disconnected support;
ordinary depth is being maximized over R^5. Formula (10) is an exact
arbitrary-mixture obstruction, not an actual convex-slice example.

## 2. Why those clusters cannot be actual one-integer slices

In fact no convex body with one integer coordinate can have a
projected mixed measure supported in the six Q_i with positive mass
in three or more differently labeled clusters. This excludes every
possible decomposition into slices, not just placing Q_i at indices i.

Each positive-volume convex fiber must lie in one Q_i. Otherwise its
interior, followed by closure, would contain positive volume outside
the disjoint closed union, contradicting projected support there.
A connected convex body contained in that disjoint union lies in a
single component. If three different cluster labels occur, choose
their corresponding integer indices in increasing order z_1<z_2<z_3.
Let the middle label be j, different from the two outer labels.
Any convex interpolation of a point from the first fiber and a point
from the last, with base z_2, belongs to the middle fiber by actual
convexity. Its barycentric coordinate lambda_j is at most 5delta/6,
because the same upper bound holds at both outer fibers by (9).
But every point of the middle fiber lies in Q_j and has lambda_j at
least 1-delta/6. These inequalities contradict delta<1.

Thus an arbitrary sharp centerpoint mixture cannot simply be declared
a projected counting law of convex-compatible one-dimensional slices.
If one takes its Cayley hull instead, the intervening actual fibers
must acquire substantial additional sets. Discarding those forced
fibers changes the projected measure.

## 3. A general parity form of the same obstruction

More generally, let T be a d-simplex with vertices v_0,...,v_d and
centroid g. Around a selection of its distinct vertices put the
closed neighborhoods Q_i=v_i+delta(T-g), where 0<delta<1/2. If an
actual convex source with n integer coordinates has projected mixed
measure supported in their union and positive mass in k different
neighborhoods, then

    k<=2^n.                                             (11)

The one-neighborhood-per-positive-fiber assertion used above still
holds: zero measure outside the closed union implies every positive
full-dimensional convex fiber lies inside it, by taking its interior
and closure. Its connectedness places it in a single component.

Suppose two positive fibers at bases z,w of the same parity have
different labels i,j. Their midpoint base is an integer vector.
Convex compatibility places their Minkowski midpoint in the actual
midpoint fiber, and this midpoint set has positive d-volume.
But every point of (Q_i+Q_j)/2 has every barycentric coordinate
at most

    1/2+d*delta/(d+1) < 1-delta/(d+1).

For coordinates i or j, use one high and one low upper bound;
all other coordinates have the still smaller upper bound
d*delta/(d+1). Hence this whole midpoint set lies outside every
Q_l, since membership in Q_l requires its l-th coordinate to be
at least 1-delta/(d+1). That contradicts the projected support.
Thus each parity class can support at most one label, proving (11).

Zero-volume original fibers do not alter the argument: the midpoint
of two positive full-dimensional fibers necessarily has positive
volume, so it cannot be discarded as a null exceptional trace.
The argument uses these quantitative convex-position neighborhoods.
It does not bound the number of arbitrary disconnected projected
components; collinear chains of translated small bodies can have
arbitrarily many such components.

## 4. Scope and verification

This is a proved obstruction to importing arbitrary mixture examples
into the convex-compatible slice class. It does not establish Gamma_d/2
for that class or bound the number of arbitrary disconnected components.
The actual many-slice Gamma_5 failure is proved separately in
`candidate 0d7a19234146a56a`.
The exact verifier is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_projected_count_density_and_cluster_obstruction.py`.
